fixes.explanation: Teaching Isaac to run things might be a fine idea, but Abraham never asks for it here. The oath is about taking a wife for his son Isaac. Nothing in these verses mentions lessons of any kind. This servant has a long trip coming, friend, and I think he'd better stretch his legs.

Relatives is it. Abraham says the servant will go to "…my country and my kindred…" and kindred means family. So Isaac's wife is to come from Abraham's own people. The servant has a family search ahead of him, friend, and I hope somebody packed extra cookies.

Neighbors is close to where Abraham says not to look. The oath rules out taking a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he is dwelling. Then he points the servant toward his own country and his kindred instead. Nice try, friend, but this search is about family, not the folks nearby.

That's the land Abraham left, friend. He says the LORD brought him from his father's house and his native land. The promise points to a different place: the LORD gives Abraham's offspring this land, the one he lives in now. Abraham also tells the servant, "Make sure that you do not take my son back there."

Yes, His angel. Abraham says the LORD, the God of heaven, "…will send His angel before you…" So the servant isn't heading out alone with ten camels and a big job. Abraham says an angel goes ahead of him on this search for a wife for Isaac.

Gates come up in plenty of Bible stories, friend, but not in this verse. The servant has the camels kneel down near the well outside the town. That's where the women go to draw water at this time of evening. Good guess, but the answer is the well.

Not quite, friend. The servant doesn't wait. After Rebekah fills her jar and comes up again, he runs to meet her and says, "Please let me have a little water from your jar." This man is on the move, and he's running.

True. Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw water. She keeps going until she has drawn water for all his camels. Ten camels and one jar, friend. I'd need a nap and a cookie just thinking about it.

She doesn't stop after one jar, friend. Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw water. She keeps at it until she has drawn water for all his camels. One jar, ten camels, and she finishes the job.

Nothing in the text says that. The servant watches Rebekah silently to see whether the LORD had made his journey a success. Payment never comes up in these verses. He's watching to see how his prayer is answered.

It's the other way around, friend. Rebekah tells him, "We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night." So there's room, and plenty for the camels too. A full house would have been a rough answer for the servant and his ten camels.

Robbers never come up in the text. The servant blesses the LORD, "…who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master." He also says the LORD has led him on the journey to the house of his master's relatives. Safety from robbers isn't part of his praise, friend.
